articles.title: Henry Pollock: Northampton fans on contract stand-off
articles.summary: How has a drawn-out and public contract negotiation affected the relationship between Henry Pollock and his fans?
articles.body:
Henry Pollock is determined not to blink first in his contractual face-off.

Despite a deal with Northampton being close, amid reports of an agreement of about £400,000 a year, , external the back row stressed on Monday that his renewal was not signed.

Asked if he was looking forward to the end of the saga, stoked by Pollock's advisor Eddie Hearn, Saints director of rugby Phil Dowson joked that "it would have been good to have it sorted three weeks ago".

The haggling has certainly played out more publicly than most negotiations.

Has it taken some of the sheen off a player who was key to Saints winning the Prem title last season and whose public profile has brought new supporters and attention, not just to his club but to his sport in general?

'The theatre around it will grind people's gears'

Lis Saunders is the chair of the Northampton Saints Supporters Group.

"I have known Henry coming up through the academy and he is absolutely delightful," she told BBC Sport.

"The perception of his arrogance is wrong. He is just a young bouncy man, living his best life.

"Some people are getting a bit fed up with the whole theatre around [the contract stand-off], though.

"I am laissez-faire about it. If he stays it will be brilliant, but you can't keep someone who wants to go.

"The whole theatre around it is what will grind people's gears. You are starting to see that on some of the fan forums – people saying, 'Either sign or don't. Just don't mess around - we don't need this drama.'"

Saunders points out that, while Pollock can pull a crowd, Saints invariably fill Franklin's Gardens anyway. The turnstiles will carry on clicking at the same rate regardless of his presence.

It would be an emotional wrench rather than a financial loss if he moves elsewhere.

"As the players themselves say, he's an idiot, but he's our idiot," said Saunders.

"We've watched him grow up and he's very much ours. It would be really sad if he didn't stay - perhaps understandable, but really sad."

Charles McGillivray is one of the hosts of Beneath the Lift Tower, , external a Northampton Saints podcast run by fans and named after the landmark that looms over Franklin's Gardens.

He says the stand-off has split fans, even if Pollock, who was superb at the end of last season, still has the support of the majority.

"There are probably two ends of the spectrum," he said.

"You've got some fans who are just reading headlines, may not be as engaged as others and don't really understand the mechanics of how rugby clubs in England work, with the salary cap and things like that.

"But most Saints fans are fairly grounded. They understand that Eddie Hearn coming to Henry Pollock's career is going to be brilliant for the sport and together they're going to make lots of noise.

"And they also understand that the money being quoted [Hearn says Pollock is worth £1m a season] isn't really feasible to be earned by someone in England.

"We think he's a grounded - if ambitious - lad and therefore Northampton is the best place for him to be.

"There isn't a club in England at the moment developing talent at the rate of knots or to the level that Northampton is. And maybe only Bath are having the continued success that Northampton are having."

McGillivray's co-host Simon Stacey, who has been following the club for 40 years, points out that Northampton fans have seen first hand the risks that players run for their rewards.

In 2018 Saints centre Rob Horne went in for a hard but routine tackle and incurred nerve damage that cost him the use of his right arm.

"I don't hold any grudges against Henry," said Stacey. "It doesn't annoy me. I get that they do need to get what they can because it's a short career and they have to look after themselves."

With a club's spending on salaries capped at £6.4m - with another £1.4m available in various credits and compensations - a bumper pay deal for one player at a Prem club reduces the money available for others.

Last autumn scrum-half Alex Mitchell said he and others had prioritised the togetherness , external and quality of Saints' squad over "mega money" elsewhere when opting to re-sign.

While Northampton did not pay up to the salary cap in the most recent report on Prem club finances, which covers the 2024-25 season, a raft of renewals is likely to take them closer to the limit in the coming years.

However, if Pollock's stance is causing ructions in the squad, they are hiding it well.

Fly-half Fin Smith momentarily joined Hearn in lobbying for Pollock to be granted a £1m annual salary this month, telling reporters that "he's worth it" before joking that Pollock had sent him out to do a bit of PR on his behalf.

Dowson dropped a request into the squad's group chat, asking if the squad could borrow the private jet Hearn had laid on for Pollock to visit him on the French Rivera.

As Pollock gave an interview on Monday, soberly stressing that the forthcoming season could be his last at the club, his straight face briefly broke as Mitchell smirked at him from across the room.

Hearn has said he found Pollock's current earnings at Northampton, thought to be about £150,000 a year, to be unbelievable. And not in a good way.

Certainly, Pollock, one of the faces of the sport, is due a significant pay raise.

The league's latest salary cap report is revealing.

His current salary is below that of the 2024-25 league average of £191,000.

Of the players in his current age bracket (20-22) that season, 27% were paid more than he is now.

Pollock has 13 England caps. The average wage of a player with 11-20 caps was £224,000.

Even if he finalises his reported extension, it will be at a lower level than the average 'marquee' player – those whose pay is excluded from the salary cap – took home in 2024-25. That figure was £533,000.

Finn Russell, the Scotland fly-half and only other rugby player who is part of Hearn's Matchroom stable, is one of those marquee players, on a deal worth about £1m a year with Bath.

Pollock has long since outgrown his current deal, signed in December 2024 before his England debut, Champions Cup knockout heroics and British and Irish Lions call-up.

The obvious destination were Pollock to move within the Prem.

Backed by Austrian energy drink dynasty, Pollock would be a statement signing that fits their youth-orientated brand. The club had plenty of headroom on the pay roll, spending barely half of the salary cap's upper limit in 2024-25 campaign.

However, a revamp of the playing squad since then will have given them less ability to manoeuvre, and Prem Rugby rules on domestic moves prevent Pollock from being the club's designated marquee player for his first two seasons elsewhere.

Pollock would also have to weigh up whether swapping the Prem champions for the league's bottom club, who are without Champions Cup rugby for 2026-27 at least, is desirable.

French clubs operate under a significantly higher salary cap of 11m euros (£9.4m), and the Top14 is booming, challenging football for prominence in the country.

Thanks to skirmishes with Bordeaux-Begles in the Champions Cup, Pollock has pantomime villain status in the country.

He was jeered the loudest of any player when England played France in Paris in March. His vigorous celebrations of Tommy Freeman's 76th-minute try, which appeared to have clinched the win for the visitors, will have further endeared him to the locals.

However, a move across the Channel would come at the cost of Pollock's England career and the associated central contract, worth about £150,000.

There is also a considerable cultural shock to overcome. Courtney Lawes, a Northampton legend, has just returned to England, saying some aspects of his two-season spell with Brive were challenging.

Henry Arundell, the bright, young thing of English rugby before Pollock, endured a difficult time at Racing 92 before returning to the Prem a year earlier than anticipated.

The money-making move of choice for many of the southern hemisphere's finest.

Richie Mo'unga, Pieter Steph du Toit and Malcolm Marx are among those who have enjoyed the lighter schedule and yen-heavy pay days in Japan.

While England internationals George Kruis and Alex Goode have made moves there in the past, there has been a shift lately to favour Japanese players over big-money imports.

Both Kruis and Goode were near the end of their careers. A switch to such relative obscurity would do little to build Pollock's brand in rugby's major markets.

Perhaps the most intriguing comment made by Pollock this week was a desire to explore "other sports" during his career.

He has been a ringside regular since signing with Matchroom, most recently attending Katie Taylor's farewell fight at Dublin's Croke Park, and chatting with UFC fighter Ian Machado Garry at a recent charity fundraising event.

His high-energy style would suit a switch to rugby league, and it has been reported , external that a number of Super League clubs, buoyed by possible investment from the NRL, are monitoring Pollock's situation.

The big-money start-up circuit, originally slated to begin next month, would surely have been keen on Pollock.

However, it has been postponed until 2028 and, with conflict in the Middle East further unsettling investors and logistics, looks increasingly unlikely to transpire.

articles.title: Tommy Freeman: England winger signs new Northampton Saints deal
articles.summary: Northampton Saints and England winger Tommy Freeman agrees a contract extension with the reigning Prem champions.
articles.body:
England winger Tommy Freeman has signed a new contract with Prem champions Northampton Saints, keeping him at Franklin's Gardens "for the foreseeable future".

The 25-year-old made his Saints debut in 2019 and has gone on to make 118 appearances for the club across all competitions, scoring 79 tries.

He scored Saints' opening try in their 2024 Premiership final win over Bath and repeated the feat in their 2026 triumph over Exeter Chiefs.

"Its a no-brainer in terms of the coaching staff we've got," Freeman told BBC Radio Northampton.

"I think I'm going to grow as a player here. I don't think anywhere else at the moment is going to help me do that.

"I'm performing with England as well and involved in that, and that's a big credit to Saints - giving me the opportunity and putting me on the stage to do my skills and go and impress."

Freeman's decision to commit his future to Saints follows on from England team-mates Fin Smith , Fraser Dingwall and Alex Mitchell also all agreeing new deals at Northampton - although the future of Henry Pollock remains uncertain.

"You can't really beat the players in and around us, the group of friends we've got, and the coaching staff to help me grow as a player," Freeman added.

"You want to be happy where you're playing. Being a special group, you go on to achieve something special as a group."

Following his England debut in the 2021 autumn internationals, Freeman has won 30 caps, scoring 11 tries. Freeman also made six appearances for the British and Irish Lions on their 2025 tour of Australia, including three Test matches.

Saints' director of rugby Phil Dowson told the club website: , external "To have Tommy commit his future to the club so early in this season's recruitment and retention cycle is a huge boost for us. We're delighted that he's chosen to continue his journey with Northampton Saints."

Freeman has played at both wing and centre for England, and Saints head coach Sam Vesty has not ruled out Freeman featuring more at full-back for his club.

"I think he'll cover more of the backline," Vesty said. "With squads getting that little bit smaller, being able to have a couple of positions to play is a fantastic attribute, and that's one of his big strengths."

The exact duration of Freeman's new deal has not been revealed although he still had one season remaining on his previous contract.

BBC Radio Northampton sports editor Graham McKechnie:

Freeman is without doubt one of Saints' crown jewels, so re-signing him is an important boost before the start of the new season.

There's been so much talk about Pollock's future at Saints, but purely in rugby terms, keeping Freeman in black, green and gold is even more important.

Not only is Freeman one of the best wingers in the world, as he's shown with both the Lions and England, but he's also an important figure off the pitch for Saints.

Like others before him, such as Smith, Mitchell and Dingwall, he's talked about the importance of the bond of friendship they have at the club.

He may well have been able to earn more elsewhere, but having that happy work environment is clearly a big deal for him and others - as well as playing a very exciting brand of rugby.

articles.title: WXV: Keira Bevan to play fly-half in Wales' opener v South Africa
articles.summary: Keira Bevan is to switch half-back roles after being selected to play at 10 for Wales' WXV opener against South Africa in Cardiff on Friday.
articles.body:
Keira Bevan will switch half-back roles after being selected to play at 10 for Wales' WXV opener against South Africa in Cardiff on Friday.

The 29-year-old has been training at fly-half during pre-season and will partner Seren Lockwood.

Wales' regular 10, Lleucu George, is named among the replacements, while Kayleigh Powell is no longer an option having been ruled out of the campaign with a hamstring injury.

Head coach Sean Lynn has included three uncapped players in his matchday squad, with Amy Williams named on the wing having impressed in a two-try display in June's uncapped Barbarians fixture.

Front row forwards Elan Jones and Shanelle Williams are poised to win first caps from the bench.

Live on BBC One, iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app, with live text coverage

Co-captains Alex Callender and Kate Williams will make a rare appearance together having overcome injuries, and are joined in the back row by Bryonie King.

Maisie Davies is given the nod ahead of Gwenllian Pyrs at loose-head prop, and packs downs in the front row with Kelsey Jones and Sisilia Tuipulotu.

Georgia Evans and Branwen Metcalfe are named as locks.

In a reshuffed back line, Lisa Neumann moves to full-back, with Seren Singleton named on the other wing.

Courtney Keight and Freya Bell form a new-look centre partnership with Carys Cox unavailable for selection.

There is no place in the matchday squad for the experienced Bethan Lewis and Hannah Dallavalle, who have both previously captained the side, while three-time Olympian Jasmine Joyce also misses out.

Lynn described his team selection as "exciting" and said the new half-back partnership had been "working very well".

"We know how much of a threat Seren was in the the Barbarians fixture and Keira has been very good in training," he said.

"When she (Bevan) played in the Bristol Bears game [at 10], she looked very comfortable there

"From being a nine, she's used to being the general and will boss that on and off the pitch and drive our attack as well."

Lynn says he is also excited by his back three, particularly Neumann at full-back.

"We've got to get Lisa Neumann with hands on ball, she is such a running threat," he added.

"She's been working on her backfield positioning and has got a pretty big boot as well, and if you're looking at the last line of defence, you don't get any more physical than Lisa Neumann."

articles.title: Amy Hardcastle: England women's all-time record try scorer announces international retirement
articles.summary: England women's all-time record try scorer Amy Hardcastle announces her international retirement.
articles.body:
England women's all-time record try scorer Amy Hardcastle has announced her international retirement.

The St Helens centre, 37, scored 30 tries in 29 appearances for her country, having made her international debut in 2009.

England head coach Stuart Barrow described her as "one of the defining players of her generation".

She leaves the international game a month before the start of the Rugby League World Cup - having featured at the past three tournaments - but will continue to play at club level.

Hardcastle was the only England player selected in the Women's Team of the Decade, picked by the NRL in 2020 to highlight the outstanding players of the 2010s.

"Representing England has been the greatest honour of my rugby league career," she said.

"To wear the national shirt, play alongside so many incredible team-mates and represent my family, clubs and community has meant everything to me.

"After a lot of reflection, I feel now is the right time to step away from the international game. I'm incredibly proud of what we've achieved and how far women's rugby league has come during my career.

"I'd like to thank every coach, team-mate, member of staff and supporter who has been part of my international journey.

"I'll be the biggest cheerleader for the girls who are selected to fly to Australia, and I wish the squad and Stuart Barrow every success at the Rugby League World Cup."

England's opening match of the World Cup is against Wales in Perth on 17 October.

Paying tribute to Hardcastle, England head coach Barrow added: "She has been an outstanding ambassador for the sport, a role model for young players and someone who has consistently driven standards on and off the field.

"Throughout her international career, Amy has shown professionalism, resilience and an unwavering commitment to the England programme.

"She has performed on the biggest stages, inspired team-mates and helped elevate the profile of women's rugby league both nationally and internationally."

articles.title: Ospreylia: How the Ospreys turned to Australia in summer recruitment drive
articles.summary: Ospreys could field a side that is a third Australian after a summer recruitment drive that brought in four players from the southern hemisphere.
articles.body:
Ospreys will have an Australian twang this season, but it was not until May that they opted to recruit from down under through necessity.

Mark Jones could pick a starting line-up that is 33% Aussie in the 2026-27 campaign, which gets under way with a United Rugby Championship (URC) fixture against Sharks in Durban on Saturday, 26 September (15:00 BST).

The Australian invasion started in the summer of 2025 when lock Ryan Smith arrived to soften the blow of losing Adam Beard to Montpellier.

He has been followed to west Wales by three Wallabies in back-row forward Liam Wright , centre Lalakai Foketi and wing Marika Koroibete, plus fly-half Lawson Creighton.

It is a recruitment drive that has excited supporters after the loss of Jac Morgan and Dewi Lake, but one that happened due to uncertainty over the club's future.

"When we were looking in the market it was May, because that was really when we got the go-ahead from the Ospreys board to start recruitment," head coach Jones told the Scrum V podcast.

"You should be done at Christmas, you shouldn't be looking in May, so some of it was necessity."

Resilient Ospreys players need certainty - Jones

Wales great Jones returns to Ospreys as a director

The first piece of the jigsaw came with Wright, who had frequently cropped up on the Queensland Reds footage that Ospreys viewed when scouting Smith.

Jones said: "Who's a guy that ticks a lot of boxes for what we need and happens to be very friendly with the lock we'd already signed?

"After that we thought that if we are going to bring three or four players in, we should probably get them from the same country for the cohesion bit.

"They all knew each other and we thought the best chance of them settling in and being happy was to recruit from the same sort of area.

"There were some other options from different parts of the world, but we felt the cohesion was something we could cash in on in terms of getting everybody up to speed quickly."

Ospreys will be "stoked" if the new quartet make an impact like Smith did in his first season.

Wales might also be watching with interest after the signing of former Wallabies captain Wright.

The 28-year-old has won six caps but, courtesy of his grandfather from Pembroke, will be eligible to play for Steve Tandy's side next summer.

That opens up the possibility of Wright targeting a World Cup spot, but the forward is concentrating on Ospreys after injury torment since a shoulder blow suffered playing against Wales in 2024.

"I know that I want to get myself back playing good enough footie and consistent enough footie to push for international honours again," he told Scrum V.

"I've always imagined that for Australia, I didn't come over here because of the Welsh heritage and trying to flip.

"But given my journey, it would be irresponsible to try and think too far ahead. I want to play good footie for Ospreys and put a lot of minutes under my belt, making sure that I am loving footie again."

Mark Jones on Liam Wright: "There is leadership - he has led Australia and been captain of the Reds. He has been incredible since coming through the door. With Liam, you are going to see composure, set-piece quality and a work rate that people will be proud of when they watch him."

On Lalakai Foketi: "A very physical player, which is so important in the URC against South African and Irish teams. You have the gain line in the winter months but he gives a nice skill set around his passing and he'll be able to use more of the width of the pitch. He is a very quiet and unassuming guy but very intellectual around the game."

On Lawson Creighton: "There aren't many outside halves that put defence down as their point of difference. He's got a very long kicking game and can attack the line really well. He played 12 most of last year because [Waratahs coach] Mike Catt felt he had those attributes, but he has slotted back at 10 really well here."

On Marika Koroibete: "Quite a bit has been made of Marika's age but the first thing you look at are his physical metrics and what he is delivering. He is probably not the 10.7 secs 100m runner that he was but he has got eight or nine high-speed efforts and is very physical. He is different to what we've got and it's about the blend. I spoke to Eddie Jones about him and Eddie was very complimentary, and that says it all."
